d: Fixed window, sliding window log, and sliding window counter
goal: Your win today: you can show the fixed-window edge exploit (10 requests through a 5/min limit), walk the sliding-log example step by step, compute a sliding-window-counter estimate (3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5) and compare all five algorithms on accuracy, memory and bursts.
bookSections: Step 2 'Algorithms for rate limiting': fixed window counter, sliding window log, sliding window counter (with pros/cons and the Cloudflare figure)

stages.title: Exploit the edge
stages.sub: Fixed window counter and its loophole
stages.teaches: Fixed window counter: divide the timeline into fixed-size windows and keep a counter per window. Each request increments the counter by one; once it reaches the threshold, new requests are dropped until the next window starts. Book example 1: window = 1 second, max 3 requests per second. Problem: a burst at the window edges lets more than the quota through. Book example 2: max 5 requests per minute, quota resets at the round minute; 5 requests between 2:00:00 and 2:01:00 and 5 more between 2:01:00 and 2:02:00 — but the one-minute span 2:00:30–2:01:30 contains 10 requests, twice the limit. Pros: memory efficient; easy to understand; resetting quota at the end of a unit fits some use cases. Cons: spikes at window edges can let through more than the quota.
stages.interaction: Timeline sim from 2:00:00 to 2:02:00, split into two 1-minute windows with counters (limit 5/min). The learner taps on the timeline to drop requests at chosen times; each one shows green (allowed) or red (dropped) and the window's counter increments. A draggable 60-second 'ruler' (a translucent band) can slide anywhere; it shows how many allowed requests fall inside it. Challenge: 'Get 10 allowed requests inside one 60-second ruler position.' Success requires placing ~5 late in window 1 and ~5 early in window 2. On success, the ruler snaps to 2:00:30–2:01:30 and the book's caption appears. A 'Show me' button auto-plays the book example for anyone stuck (no XP).
stages.check: Challenge solved or auto-played; quiz: 'Limit 5/min, fixed windows. Max requests that can pass in some 60-second span?' → 10.

stages.title: Keep a log
stages.sub: Sliding window log, step by step
stages.teaches: Sliding window log fixes the edge problem by tracking each request's timestamp, usually in a cache such as a Redis sorted set (a set ordered by a score — here the timestamp). On a new request: remove all timestamps older than the start of the current window (now − window length); add the new request's timestamp to the log; if the log size is ≤ the allowed count, accept, otherwise reject. Book example (limit 2 requests per minute): 1:00:01 — log empty, accepted. 1:00:30 — log size 2, accepted. 1:00:50 — log size 3 > 2, rejected, but its timestamp stays in the log. 1:01:40 — window is [1:00:40, 1:01:40); 1:00:01 and 1:00:30 are outdated and removed; log is [1:00:50, 1:01:40], size 2 → accepted. Pros: very accurate — in any rolling window, requests never exceed the limit. Cons: lots of memory, since it stores a timestamp per request, even rejected ones.
stages.interaction: Step-through predict game. A log panel (vertical list of timestamp chips) and a clock. For each of the four book requests, the learner first taps 'Accept' or 'Reject', then the sim plays the three steps visibly: grey out and remove expired chips, add the new chip, compare size vs limit. Correct predictions earn XP. On request 3, a highlighted note shows the rejected chip staying in the log. On request 4, the learner must also tap which chips will be evicted (1:00:01 and 1:00:30) before the animation. Finally a memory meter: 'Limit 500/hour, 1M users, each timestamp ~8 bytes' → learner computes worst-case log memory ≈ 500 × 8 B × 1M = 4 GB (accept 3.5–4.5 GB), to make the memory con concrete.
stages.check: Four predictions + the eviction pick + the memory estimate; quiz: 'Why does the log use more memory than it seems to need?' → it stores timestamps even for rejected requests.

stages.title: Blend two windows
stages.sub: Sliding window counter: calculate and check
stages.teaches: Sliding window counter is a hybrid of fixed window counter and sliding log. Estimate requests in the rolling window = requests in current window + requests in previous window × overlap percentage of the rolling window and the previous window. Book example: limit 7 per minute, 5 requests in the previous minute, 3 in the current; a new request arrives 30% into the current minute → 3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5, rounded down to 6 (round up or down depending on the use case) → under 7, so the request goes through; the limit will be reached after one more. Pros: smooths spikes because the rate uses the average of the previous window; memory efficient (two counters per key). Cons: only works for a not-so-strict look-back window; it is an approximation that assumes requests in the previous window were evenly spread. Cloudflare's experiments: only 0.003% of requests were wrongly allowed or rate limited among 400 million requests.
stages.interaction: Slider calculator. A bar shows the previous window (5 requests) and current window (3 requests) with a 60-second rolling band whose position is controlled by a slider (0–100% into the current minute). Live readout: overlap % with previous = 100 − position; estimate = current + previous × overlap. Then 4 calculate-and-check rounds where the learner types the estimate and Allow/Reject (rule shown: round down; allow if estimate < limit): R1 book example (limit 7, prev 5, cur 3, 30%) → 6.5 → 6 → allow. R2 limit 10, prev 8, cur 4, 25% → 4 + 8×0.75 = 10 → reject. R3 limit 10, prev 8, cur 4, 75% → 4 + 2 = 6 → allow. R4 limit 100, prev 120, cur 30, 50% → 30 + 60 = 90 → allow. After R4, a 'What if' card: previous window's 5 requests all came in its last second — the estimate still says 3.5, but reality had 5 in the rolling window: the approximation's blind spot.
stages.check: At least 3 of 4 rounds correct for full XP; quiz: 'What does sliding window counter assume about the previous window?' → its requests were evenly distributed.

stages.title: The algorithm draft
stages.teaches: Summary from the book: token bucket (easy, memory efficient, allows bursts; two params hard to tune; Amazon, Stripe). Leaking bucket (memory efficient, fixed outflow; bursts fill the queue with old requests, two params; Shopify). Fixed window counter (memory efficient, easy, resets at round times; edge spikes). Sliding window log (very accurate; memory hungry). Sliding window counter (smooths spikes, memory efficient; approximate, assumes even distribution).
stages.interaction: Matching board: 5 algorithm columns; 10 shuffled trait cards (each algorithm's main pro and main con). The learner taps a card then a column. Wrong placements shake and cost no heart but no XP for that card. When done, the board turns into a reference table that stays visible. Then a 'Which would you pick?' mini-round with 3 one-line situations: 'must be exact, small user base' → sliding window log; 'billions of keys, approximate is fine' → sliding window counter; 'quota resets at midnight for a daily plan' → fixed window.

stages.title: Boss: The Clock Wraith
stages.teaches: Applying the window algorithms under interview pressure.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 5 scenarios. Examples: 'A user gets 2× their per-minute quota through by timing calls around :00. Which algorithm are you on?' → fixed window counter; 'Fix it with the least memory' → sliding window counter (not sliding log); 'Auditors require that no rolling 60-second span ever exceeds the limit' → sliding window log; 'Sliding log memory exploded during an attack. Why?' → rejected requests are still logged; 'Cloudflare's sliding window counter was wrong for what share of 400M requests?' → 0.003%.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Interview-ready comparison of the three window algorithms.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Walk me through fixed window, sliding log, and sliding window counter — and which you'd ship.' Model answer: fixed window counts per round window, cheap, but edges allow 2× (5/min → 10 in 2:00:30–2:01:30); sliding log stores timestamps in a sorted set, exact, but memory-heavy including rejected ones; sliding window counter = current + previous × overlap (3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5), two counters per key, approximate (Cloudflare 0.003% error); ship sliding window counter or token bucket for most APIs, sliding log when exactness matters and volumes are small. Checks: edge problem with numbers; log memory con; the formula; a reasoned pick.

caveats: The book says round 6.5 'down' in its example but notes you could round either way; real implementations vary (Cloudflare compares the unrounded weighted rate to the limit).
The 0.003% figure comes from Cloudflare's own traffic; other traffic shapes (very bursty clients) can make the approximation worse.

The book's sliding log adds a rejected request's timestamp to the log. Some implementations only log accepted requests, which saves memory but means a client that keeps hammering isn't penalized for the rejected attempts.
